newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Speaker Gingrich blames press for ethics heat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Speaker Gingrich blames press for ethics heat.

text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Saturday that the press was partly responsible for his ethics troubles, telling hundreds of cheering supporters that he could not speak openly on the subject without risking fresh attacks from Democrats and the media.

Appearing at a town hall meeting in his home district, the Georgia Republican told a packed auditorium that his opponents wanted to keep public attention on his unprecedented reprimand and $300,000 penalty in order to avoid talking about the "things that really matter," namely the Republican legislative agenda.
"The No. 1 focus we have for the next five weeks is to pass the constitutional amendment to require a balanced budget," Gingrich said to sustained applause from about 500 supporters.

"At an appropriate time, I want to give a speech that will walk through the whole (ethics) situation. I don't want to get involved in a specific point-by-point, because I'll say something here and our friends in the press will run to someone else," he said in a reference to House Democrats including his arch nemesis, Representative David Bonior of Michigan, the Democratic party whip.

"You'll then end up with eight seconds of what I might have said, two minutes of David Bonior distorting what was going on and the Atlanta Constitution then writing an editorial making up totally false statements," he said.
Gingrich staff distributed handouts on the ethics issue, which the speaker said would avoid "a whole new wave of controversy, which is the thing that our opponents would most like."

The handouts were three Jan. 17 memos that Ohio Republican Representative John Boehner, a staunch Gingrich ally, provided for House Republicans as part of a coordinated counterattack against adverse publicity from the speaker's ethics case.

The documents said Gingrich was not found in violation of U.S. tax laws by the House ethics panel, claimed the speaker's missteps had been nothing as serious as the scandals that have rocked the White House and warned readers to expect "hot rhetoric and gross exaggeration" from the speaker's opponents.

The meeting came as the 53-year-old conservative and his allies struggled to weather a storm of controversy in Washington raised by a scathing House Ethics Committee report and Tuesday's 395-28 vote to reprimand him and impose a $300,000 penalty.

Under an effective plea-bargain arrangement, the committee made no finding as to whether Gingrich used tax-exempt funds illegally for partisan political purposes in the form of his college course, entitled "Renewing American Civilisation." But the former history professor admitted he should have sought legal advice on the question.

The biggest task now before Gingrich was to find a way to pay his six-figure penalty that would not arouse a new furore as the House began a new session. Many members of Congress have said Gingrich should not take the money from his campaign warchest.

The speaker already has turned away at least $300,000 in voluntary pledges from callers around the country, according to his staff. Such donations would be considered campaign funds under U.S. election law.
"We're getting hundreds of calls a day, and maybe two are negative," said Nancy Desmond, director of Gingrich's office in Marietta, Georgia.
